segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the whole assembly of them rose and brought him before Pilate.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They began to accuse him, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “We found this man leading our nation astray, forbidding people to pay taxes to Caesar, and saying that he himself is Messiah, a king.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Pilate asked him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Are you the king of the Jews?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He answered him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “You say so.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Pilate said to the chief priests and the crowds,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I find no ground for a charge in this man.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But they kept insisting,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “He stirs up the people, teaching throughout all Judea, starting from Galilee and all the way to here.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Pilate heard this, he asked whether the man was a Galilean,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and on learning that he came under Herod’s jurisdiction, he sent him over to Herod, who was himself also in Jerusalem in those days.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Herod saw Jesus he was very glad, for he had been wanting to see him for a considerable time because of what he had heard about him, and he was hoping to see some sign done by him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He questioned him at considerable length, but Jesus gave him no answer.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The chief priests and the scribes stood by, vehemently accusing him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Herod too, with his troops, treated him with contempt and mocked him; then, putting a splendid robe on him, he sent him back to Pilate.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: That very day Herod and Pilate became friends with each other; before this they had been at enmity.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Pilate called together the chief priests, the rulers, and the people,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and said to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You brought this man to me as one who was turning the people to revolt. Look, I examined him in your presence and found in this man no ground for the charges you bring against him.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Nor did Herod, for he sent him back to us. Look, he has done nothing deserving death.

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: So I will discipline him and release him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But they all cried out together,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Away with this man! Release Barabbas for us!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: This was a man who had been thrown into prison because of an uprising that had taken place in the city, and for murder.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Pilate addressed them again, wanting to release Jesus,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but they kept shouting,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Crucify, crucify him!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: A third time he said to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Why? What evil has this man done? I have found in him no ground for a death sentence. So I will discipline him and release him.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But they kept pressing him with loud voices, asking that he be crucified, and their voices prevailed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So Pilate ruled that their request should be granted.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He released the man they asked for, the one who had been thrown into prison for uprising and murder, and Jesus he handed over to their will.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As they led him away, they seized a certain Simon of Cyrene, who was coming in from the country, and laid the cross on him to carry behind Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: A great number of the people followed him, and among them women who were mourning and lamenting for him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Jesus turned to them and said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me; weep rather for yourselves and for your children,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: for look, days are coming when people will say, ‘Blessed are the barren, the wombs that never gave birth and the breasts that never nursed.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Then they will begin to say to the mountains, ‘Fall on us,’ and to the hills, ‘Cover us.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For if they do these things when the wood is green, what will happen when it is dry?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Two others, criminals, were also being led away to be put to death with him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they came to the place called the Skull, they crucified him there, along with the criminals, one on his right and one on his left.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And Jesus was saying,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they cast lots to divide his clothes among them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The people stood watching. The rulers too were sneering at him, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “He saved others; let him save himself, if this is the Messiah of God, the Chosen One.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The soldiers also mocked him, coming up and offering him sour wine

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “If you are the king of the Jews, save yourself!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: There was also an inscription over him: “This is the King of the Jews.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: One of the criminals hanging there kept insulting him:

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Are you not the Messiah? Save yourself and us!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the other answered, rebuking him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Do you not even fear God, since you are under the same sentence?

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: And we justly, for we are getting what our deeds deserve; but this man has done nothing wrong.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Jesus, remember me when you come in your kingdom.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Truly I tell you, today you will be with me in paradise.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It was now about the sixth hour, and darkness came over the whole land until the ninth hour,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: as the sun’s light failed; and the curtain of the temple was torn down the middle.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then Jesus called out with a loud voice,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Father, into your hands I entrust my spirit.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Having said this, he breathed his last.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the centurion saw what had happened, he glorified God, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Surely this man was righteous.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And all the crowds who had gathered for this spectacle, after watching what took place, returned beating their breasts.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: All who knew him were standing at a distance, and so were the women who had followed him from Galilee, seeing these things.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now there was a man named Joseph, a member of the council, a good and righteous man—

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: he had not agreed with their decision and their action—from Arimathea, a town of the Jews, and he was waiting for the kingdom of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: This man went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He took it down, wrapped it in a linen cloth, and laid him in a tomb cut in the rock, where no one had yet been laid.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: It was the day of Preparation, and the Sabbath was about to begin.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The women who had come with him from Galilee followed and saw the tomb and how his body was laid.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then they returned and prepared spices and perfumed oils. On the Sabbath they rested according to the commandment.

notes.note: The Greek word here is the same one that, in the plural, is usually translated “Gentiles” when it refers to the non-Jewish peoples. In the singular and used of Israel, as here, it simply means a people or nation. Dividing the word by sense in this way is standard practice.

The Greek word means “anointed” and was the title of the king Israel expected. Where the title itself is the point, as in this accusation, the translation uses “Messiah” and keeps “Christ” where the word works as a name; several modern translations make the same split. The phrase could also be read “an anointed king.” Either way the charge is framed so that a Roman governor would hear a rival to Caesar.

The verb ordinarily means to train or correct a child. In a governor’s mouth it is a mild word for a beating given as a warning before release, and some translations say outright “have him flogged.” The rendering keeps Pilate’s understated term; the same word recurs in verse 22.

There is no verse 17 in the Greek text translated here. The words “Now he was obliged to release one prisoner to them at the festival” are missing from the earliest manuscripts and appear at different places in others. They are generally regarded as a later explanatory addition drawn from the parallel accounts in Matthew and Mark.

The saying is proverbial; literally, “if they do these things in the green wood, what will happen in the dry?” The usual understanding is that if such a fate falls on one who is innocent, like green wood that resists fire, far worse awaits a city ripe for judgment. Who “they” are is not stated and is disputed.

Luke gives only the Greek name of the place and omits the Aramaic name Golgotha that the other Gospels record. The familiar “Calvary” comes from the Latin word for skull used in the Latin Bible. Why the place had this name is not known.

notes.phrase: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.”
notes.note: This prayer is absent from several of the earliest and most important manuscripts and present in others of comparable age. Scholars are divided on whether Luke wrote it and some copyists removed it, or whether it is a very early tradition added to the Gospel. It is translated here as part of the text, as in the Greek edition followed.

notes.phrase: when you come in your kingdom
notes.traditional: when you come into your kingdom
notes.note: Manuscripts divide between “into your kingdom” and “in your kingdom”; the Greek edition translated here prints the second. “In your kingdom” most naturally means “when you come as king,” looking to a future arrival in royal power, though the Greek preposition can also be used loosely for “into.” On the first reading, Jesus’s “today” in the next verse answers a request about the distant future with something immediate.

notes.phrase: today you will be with me
notes.traditional: To day shalt thou be with me
notes.note: Ancient Greek manuscripts had no punctuation, so “today” could in principle go with “I tell you” (“Truly I tell you today, you will be with me”). Nearly all scholars take it with what follows. “Truly I tell you” is a fixed formula that nowhere else takes a time word, and “today” answers the criminal’s “when.”

Hours were counted from sunrise, so the sixth hour is about midday and the ninth about three in the afternoon. The word translated “land” can also mean “earth”; the Greek does not settle whether the darkness is local or universal.

The verb means to fail or give out and was also the ordinary term for an eclipse. An astronomical solar eclipse cannot occur at Passover, which falls at full moon, so the rendering does not specify one. Many later manuscripts read instead “and the sun was darkened,” which is the basis of the traditional wording.

Greek has one word-family where English has two (righteous and just), and this adjective can also mean “innocent.” After Pilate’s repeated findings of no guilt, “innocent” is at least part of the sense here, and many modern translations use it. “Righteous” is kept because Luke uses the same word of Joseph in verse 50 and, in Acts, calls Jesus “the Righteous One.”

“Preparation” was the usual name for Friday, the day on which everything was made ready for the Sabbath. The Sabbath began at sunset, which is why the burial is hurried and the women wait. The Greek verb translated “was about to begin” literally means “was dawning,” used here loosely of the day’s onset in the evening.

candidates.reason: Recurs throughout the Gospels and Acts; “scribes” suggests copyists to modern readers, while “experts in the law” or “teachers of the law” are common alternatives, so one decision is needed.
Ranges over heal, rescue and save in the theological sense across the New Testament, and here the taunt plays on that range; varying English would hide the links.
Covers both abusive speech against people and blasphemy against God; translators split between “blaspheme”, “revile” and “insult”, and a consistent policy by sense is needed.
Denotes the sanctuary building proper as distinct from the wider temple precincts (ἱερόν); whether to mark the distinction in English (“sanctuary” versus “temple”) should be decided once.

candidates.rendering: look (in speech); omitted or “now” in narrative
candidates.reason: Extremely frequent; renderings vary between “behold”, “look”, “see” and omission, and readers will notice inconsistency across books.
